<reason>Both sides ran competent, well-grounded cases built on plausible background knowledge (Bracero, Huelva, EU-Turkey, Hungary, 1986 legalization). PRO edges it on the decisive clashes: (1) the pressure question demanding a scaled seasonal program was answered squarely with Bracero's order-of-magnitude growth and Canada's program, while CON's counter that "no version survives scale" was left undercut; (2) PRO's asymmetry answer—that a permit subtracts a crossing while enforcement only relocates it—survived CON's "manufactures an applicant" rejoinder, which rested on assertion rather than evidence; (3) PRO's closing dismantled CON's 1986 magnet example by noting it was an amnesty for people already inside, the motion's opposite; and (4) PRO's demand-intact concession extraction ("leaves the stock of jobs-for-smugglers untouched") gave a coherent throughline. CON's best moments—the enforcement-inside-the-pathway hierarchy, the overstay pipeline, the "one tool deters, the other recruits" framing—kept the debate close, and CON's Balkan corridor answer to the land-border question was credible but confounded. PRO's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a minor execution cost, but the argumentation was substantially complete. On weighing and progression, PRO made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 2 A2 answer: confronting CON's displacement double-standard question head-on with the asymmetry claim (enforcement displacement keeps the person irregular; a permit subtracts them entirely, and rejected applicants were already coming), which CON spent its closing attacking ("manufactures an applicant") but never empirically overturned.</best_rebuttal>
